examples.name: Sample — strike
paragraphs: Every Current Rates figure is struck through, with its live replacement in the Proposed Rates tables alongside: 54 struck values across two tables. Each struck value is wrapped in ~~…~~, and the four blocks stay four tables.
Note what the page itself does: it splits old and new into parallel tables, so the replacement is not in the same cell. The output follows the page and does not fold them together.

examples.name: Sample — an interlineated court rule
paragraphs: Paragraph (4): [Deleted.] struck through in red, followed by red underlined replacement text; everything above it is plain black. Strike and underline already carry the revision, so the red adds nothing a strike and an underline do not.

snippets.text: (4) ~~\[Deleted.\]~~ <u>Unless otherwise agreed to by the parties or otherwise provided by court order or by law, only the witness, the parties, their respective counsel including such counsel's staff, experts identified pursuant to Rule 4:1(b)(4)(A), and those involved with the administration of the deposition (such as court reporters and translators) may attend the deposition, given the private nature of discovery. Counsel of record for the parties and counsel for any non-party deponent must timely confer regarding any other person's attendance at a deposition</u>

examples.name: Sample — insertions marked by colour alone
paragraphs: Proposed rule text: deletions (then, make this designation) struck through in black, insertions in red with no underline. Without the colour the insertions become indistinguishable from the settled text, so the colour is kept. The colour is written as <font color="red"> around the inserted words, as Text Colors§7.3.12 requires.

snippets.text: (6) <u>Notice or Subpoena Directed to an Organization</u>. In its notice or subpoena, a party may name as the deponent a public or private corporation, a partnership, an association, a governmental agency, or other entity and must describe with reasonable particularity the matters for examination. The named organization must ~~then~~ designate one or more officers, directors, or managing agents, or designate other persons who consent to testify on its behalf; and it may set out the matters on which each person designated will testify. <font color="red">Before or promptly after the notice or subpoena is served, the serving party and the organization must confer in good faith about the matters for examination.</font> A subpoena must advise a nonparty organization of its duty to <font color="red">confer with the serving party and to designate each person who will testify</font> ~~make this designation~~. The persons designated must testify about information known or reasonably available to the organization. This paragraph (6) does not preclude a deposition by any other procedure allowed by these rules.

examples.rendered: (6) Notice or Subpoena Directed to an Organization. In its notice or subpoena, a party may name as the deponent a public or private corporation, a partnership, an association, a governmental agency, or other entity and must describe with reasonable particularity the matters for examination. The named organization must then designate one or more officers, directors, or managing agents, or designate other persons who consent to testify on its behalf; and it may set out the matters on which each person designated will testify. Before or promptly after the notice or subpoena is served, the serving party and the organization must confer in good faith about the matters for examination. A subpoena must advise a nonparty organization of its duty to confer with the serving party and to designate each person who will testify make this designation. The persons designated must testify about information known or reasonably available to the organization. This paragraph (6) does not preclude a deposition by any other procedure allowed by these rules.
